summary: Mobility is stabilising at a near‑normal MF‑Index of 72, with public transport usage modestly below pre‑pandemic levels and fuel prices remaining high. However, actual fuel savings from the work‑from‑home mandate are far below the theoretical ceiling, and high‑mobility sectors continue to pose economic and equity risks.

signals.detail: The theoretical ceiling of 35.7 M L/week saved is not being realised; only 334 k L were reported in the first week of the mandate, representing less than 1 % of the modelled target. This gap undermines the intended fuel‑conservation benefits despite a perfect fuel‑policy component score.

Daily PT trips stand at 1.24 M, roughly 14 % below the pre‑pandemic daily average (~1.43 M). The ridership component of the MF‑Index remains at 72.7, indicating moderate recovery but still short of the 2019 baseline.

Logistics, construction and retail & services exhibit mobility scores above 85 with WFH adoption under 15 %, signalling high exposure to congestion, fuel cost volatility and labour productivity risks as the economy re‑opens.

WFH adoption varies widely—from 60 % in public & GLCs to just 5 % in construction—creating uneven exposure to fuel price shocks and mobility constraints. The current policy framework does not sufficiently address these sectoral disparities.

Elevated fuel prices (RON95 RM4.52/L) could incentivise a shift toward public transport, yet ridership has not fully rebounded. Targeted fare subsidies and service enhancements are needed to translate price pressure into lasting modal change.

recommendation: Introduce a tiered incentive scheme that rewards sectors achieving >30 % WFH with fuel tax credits, while expanding subsidised PT fares for high‑mobility workers. Set a concrete target to raise actual weekly fuel savings to 5 % of the theoretical ceiling (≈1.8 M L) within six months, and aim for a 10 % increase in daily PT trips by Q4 2027.
